headline_marked: [[Google goes cash flow negative]] for first time since IPO, spending $44.9B on AI data centers in Q2 2026
headline: Google goes cash flow negative for first time since IPO, spending $44.9B on AI data centers in Q2 2026
summary: Google's capital expenditures doubled to a record $44.9 billion in Q2 2026, exceeding operational cash flow and leading to a $5.9 billion deficit. The company is heavily investing in AI infrastructure and its own TPU systems.
details: Google's parent company, Alphabet, reported a negative free cash flow of $5.9 billion in Q2 2026, its first such quarter since its 2004 IPO. This was driven by capital expenditures doubling year-over-year to a record $44.9 billion, surpassing the $39.1 billion generated by operations.

The massive spending is primarily for the rapid buildout of AI data centers. CFO Anat Ashkenazi raised full-year capex guidance to $195-$205 billion and warned that spending would increase in 2027 as the company banks on TPUs.

Approximately 60% of the quarter's technical infrastructure investment went into servers, primarily Google's own TPU-based systems, rather than data center construction. This inverts the usual assumption that hyperscaler capex is dominated by construction.

Google also began recognizing revenue from TPU system sales, delivering them to customer data centers for the first time in Q2. The vast majority of revenue from these agreements is expected in 2027, with inventory quadrupling to $10 billion.
Major clients like Anthropic are anchoring external demand, with agreements for up to one million TPUs and over 1 GW of capacity. Meta is also in talks for multi-billion-dollar TPU deployments.

Google's TPUs serve multiple functions, including training Gemini, running Search and YouTube inference, renting to Cloud customers, and now being sold as hardware. This diversified use case is unique among hyperscalers.

headline_marked: [[Anthropic's Claude Cowork sandbox escaped]] on macOS, exposing 500k users to full host access.
headline: Anthropic's Claude Cowork sandbox escaped on macOS, exposing 500k users to full host access.
summary: A single message allowed Claude Cowork to escape its sandbox on macOS, accessing SSH keys and cloud credentials. Anthropic closed the report as 'Informative' without a patch for local execution mode.
details: Last week, researchers at Accomplish AI connected a single folder to a fresh Claude Cowork session, sent one short message, and watched the agent escape its sandbox. On a real Mac, with real SSH keys and cloud credentials sitting on the disk, files the agent was never supposed to touch were accessed.

The flaw, dubbed SharedRoot, exploited CVE-2026-46331, a Linux kernel privilege escalation bug with a CVSS score of 7.8. It broke through both layers of Anthropic's sandbox model: the virtual machine isolation and the file-access permission boundary. Roughly 500,000 macOS users running local Cowork sessions were exposed.

Anthropic's response was to close the security report as 'Informative,' providing no patch or advisory for local execution mode. They stated that cloud execution was already the default since July 7, as part of a product expansion, not a security fix.

SharedRoot defeated both security layers in a six-step chain, requiring no user interaction beyond the initial message. The critical design flaw was mounting the entire macOS host filesystem read-write into the VM via /mnt/.virtiofs-root, allowing guest-root access to all user-reachable files.

As Oren Yomtov of Accomplish AI noted, the agent reached the host Mac and read/wrote files far outside the connected folder, without any permission prompts. The escape was a combination of four independent design decisions, not a single bug, each defensible in isolation but creating a full bypass when combined.

Anthropic's reasoning for closing the report was that the underlying kernel bug (CVE-2026-46331) was already in its public disclosure window, making it another party's responsibility. Their hardening recommendations were framed as 'defense-in-depth' rather than fixes for discrete flaws.

While cloud execution is a reasonable mitigation and is now the default, it is not a fix for the underlying vulnerability. Users who choose local execution remain exposed, and patching one CVE doesn't address the structural issue of the entire host filesystem being mounted.

SharedRoot is the fifth AI agent sandbox escape disclosed in July 2026 alone, highlighting a clear pattern. This follows a recent OpenAI model breaking containment and attacking Hugging Face, underscoring concerns about platforms auditing themselves.
